The T-matrix equations are derived using a conserved-flux integral that remains invariant under deformation of the integration surface, provided no singularities are enclosed.
For dielectric objects, tangential electric and magnetic fields on the surface are represented by a single expansion, reducing computational effort by about half.
In the low-frequency limit, the electromagnetic scattering equations reduce to static potential theory equations.
Numerical results show that the present method can reduce the number of equations and unknowns by up to an order of magnitude compared to other approaches for a given accuracy.
New exact relations are established between electrostatic and magnetostatic problems using the matrix method.
The electrostatic problem is formulated by expanding the induced potential in singular spherical harmonics and enforcing constant potential boundary conditions on the surface.
The magnetostatic problem requires the normal component of magnetic induction to vanish on the surface, with induced potentials expanded similarly to the electrostatic case.
The electromagnetic scattering problem uses vector spherical wave functions (magnetic and electric multipoles) for expanding incident and scattered fields.
Orthogonality of spherical harmonics and vector spherical wave functions is fundamental to deriving matrix elements and ensuring solution completeness.
The T-matrix relates incident field expansion coefficients to scattered field coefficients, encapsulating the scattering characteristics of the object.
The method avoids the use of fictitious interior fields and the Huygens principle, which can cause conceptual difficulties in penetrable objects.
Absorption cross sections for lossy dielectric objects can be computed directly from energy balance without volume integration of field intensities.
The expansions for fields inside and outside the scatterer converge in the mean square sense and are differentiable on the surface, ensuring physical validity.
The method applies to objects of arbitrary shape without relying on the Rayleigh hypothesis, which assumes field expansions converge everywhere.
The approach unifies potential theory and electromagnetic scattering under a single matrix formalism.
